newsitem.title: USA: Dollar, still bullish, ends mostly higher in US.
newsitem.headline: Dollar, still bullish, ends mostly higher in US.

text.p: The dollar ended mostly higher on Monday, scoring good gains versus the yen and sterling while retreating only marginally versus the mark against which it had set a 7-1/2 year high in early trade.
Dollar/mark cleared 1.8430, the 1991 peak, to surge to 1.8490, its highest since November 1989 when that pair climbed as high as 1.8690. The 1989 cycle topped out at 2.0478.

The dollar rally, so far largely against the European currencies, was helped this time by a rise versus the yen. Dollar/yen went through a key resistance level at 117.00 to hit a 10-week high of 117.90 and is now targeting 119.00.
Late Monday, the dollar traded at 1.8415/25 marks versus 1.8422/32 at the open and at 117.78/88 yen vs. 117.00/10.

"It's still a continuing move higher. I think it can run to 1.85 to 1.90 marks," said Tom Benfer, director of foreign exchange at Bank of Montreal who added the rally should go unfazed if the upcoming economic data deliver no surprise.
Traders said uncertainty about the single European currency continued to weigh on the mark while positive U.S. economic fundamentals remained supportive of the dollar.
The Employment Cost Index and Gross Domestic Product for April-June are due out on Tuesday and Thursday, respectively.

Another U.S. report that may impact U.S. assets and the dollar will be the July jobs data, set for release on Friday. Traders agreed the stellar performance of U.S. bonds and stocks remained an important factor for the dollar.

"People want to be careful because they don't want to see any surprises," Benfer said. "If the inflation number picks up a bit that may help the dollar but it will not be good for the bond and stock markets."
Meanwhile, sterling tumbled about five pfennigs amid profit-taking versus the mark and speculations that U.K. interest rates may remain steady on the near term.
Sterling ended at $1.6335/45 versus $1.6510/20 at the open. Amid talk that hedge funds were selling sterling/marks actively, that cross fell from a high of 3.0627 to a low of 3.0070.
"The (sterling) market was well overbought, so in that type of situation, the risk is to the downside," said James Powers, vice president at Westdeutsche Landesbank Girozentrale.
Although a sterling/mark retreat may weigh on dollar/mark in the near term as well, dealers were confident the dollar still had more upside, possibly all the way to 2.00 marks.
Dealers also agreed the dollar/mark rally was pinned to concern that core European countries may fail to meet fiscal austerity measures needed to ensure the 1999 euro launch.
Technical analysts were predicting that dollar/yen, long a lagger, will now lead a new dollar rally. A key level is 119.00, the 50-percent retracement of the 1997 high/low move from 126.47 to 110.62.

Another leader may be dollar/Swiss which soared to 1.5250, its highest since August 1993. Further dollar/Swiss gains to 1.5520, the high in March 1993 cannot be ruled out and may be helped by a breach 0.82 support on mark/Swiss.
In other trades on Monday, the Australian dollar was quoted at $0.7365/70 versus $0.7352/57 at the open.
The U.S. dollar also ended virtually flat versus the Canadian dollar at C$1.3849/54 from C$1.3850/55, and at 1.5133/38 Swiss francs vs. 1.5163/68.
